column3: the file name the workflow gives the built program, and the name
windows/build.py then looks for in --bin. A base name, never a
directory: the packager matches a --bin file to its own payload row
by base name, and installer/payload.tsv is the only file that says
where anything lands under the install folder

column2: a Go module path and a version that is a tag on its repository.

column3: A commit is not allowed here and neither is a branch: this package
consumes our published tags exactly as a stranger does, so a module
we broke turns this workflow red on the day it is released rather
than on the day somebody outside tries to install it.
The workflow asks proxy.golang.org, which serves a version for good
once it has cached it and so cannot tell a live tag from a deleted
one. `git ls-remote --tags` on the repository can, and is what
decides whether a version may be written here

column2: the package to build, relative to the module. "." is the module

column3: root. It is a separate column because the proxy indexes modules and
not packages: asking it for .../go/cmd/dl answers 404 whatever the
version, and a check that cannot tell that from a deleted tag is
not a check

column2: service | tools — the WiX feature that installs it
console | windows. "windows" appends -H=windowsgui to the link,

column3: which is the only way to build an image the loader gives no
console, and it is also what says the row is a Windows image and
nothing else: the Linux and macOS jobs skip such a row by name
rather than building an ELF or a Mach-O nobody asked for
